summary: This document describes how to handle Unicode strings that represent memorable, friendly names, called nicknames, display names or petnames, for people, devices, accounts and websites. It obsoletes RFC 7700.

eli5.summary: It makes rules for how computers treat the fun names people choose, in any language, so they can be shown and compared properly.

questions: what is a precis nickname profile
subtitle: How to prepare, enforce and compare Unicode nicknames and display names so they behave sensibly everywhere.

tldr.problem: People pick memorable names for chat participants, devices, accounts and websites, and those names can contain any Unicode character. Without shared rules, two systems may treat the same name differently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8266 defines the Nickname profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass. It tidies spaces, maps case when comparing, and applies Unicode Normalization Form KC, and two names match only if the results are identical octet for octet.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7700. Applications still decide where nicknames appear and must base authentication and authorization on the underlying identity, never on the nickname.

today: RFC 8266 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7700. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Nicknames Need Rules
sections.content:
Many applications let a person choose a memorable, human-friendly name, or set one for something else such as a device, account, contact or website. These go by several names: nicknames in chat rooms, display names in Internet mail, and petnames. The RFC calls them all nicknames.

Chat technologies such as IRC, MSRP, XCON and XMPP support nicknames. Newer ones allow code points outside the ASCII range, usually through Unicode. Nicknames are mostly for display, but they are sometimes used programmatically too, for example to kick a user out of a chat room or to avoid nickname conflicts.

The RFC builds its rules on the PRECIS framework (preparation, enforcement and comparison of internationalized strings) defined in RFC 8264.
sections.eli5: Everyone picks their own nickname, in any alphabet. If computers do not agree how to read them, a name could look the same to you but different to the computer.

sections.title: The Nickname Rules
sections.content:
The Nickname profile is built on the PRECIS FreeformClass. It has five rules.

  • Width mapping: none, because width mapping happens as part of normalization.
  • Additional mapping: turn any non-ASCII space (general category Zs) into SPACE (U+0020), remove ASCII spaces at the start and end, and collapse runs of interior spaces into one. So "stpeter " becomes "stpeter" and "St Peter" becomes "St Peter".
  • Case mapping: apply the Unicode toLowerCase() operation.
  • Normalization: apply Unicode Normalization Form KC (NFKC), which matches more aggressively than other forms. For example, ROMAN NUMERAL FOUR (U+2163) matches the letters I and V together.
  • Directionality: none. A nickname may be shown differently in left-to-right and right-to-left layouts, as long as each layout is consistent.

Applying these rules is not idempotent for every code point. An implementation SHOULD reapply the rules until the output is stable. If it is still changing after three additional applications, it SHOULD stop and reject the input as invalid.
sections.eli5: Imagine tidying a name tag: squash extra gaps, make all letters small, and swap fancy look-alike characters for plain ones. Sometimes one tidy-up reveals another, so you repeat until nothing changes.

sections.title: Preparation, Enforcement and Comparison
sections.content:
Preparation: an entity MUST make sure the string consists only of code points allowed by the FreeformClass in RFC 8264.

Enforcement: the entity MUST prepare the string, then apply the additional mapping rule followed by the normalization rule. It SHOULD apply case mapping only during comparison. Afterwards it MUST check that the nickname is not zero bytes long, because a non-empty input can become empty after canonicalization. Until enforcement is complete, the string MUST NOT be treated as conforming.

Comparison: prepare each string, then apply additional mapping, case mapping and normalization, in that order. The two strings are equivalent if and only if they match exactly, octet for octet. Until the comparison finishes, they MUST NOT be treated as equivalent.
sections.eli5: To keep a name, you tidy spacing and look-alike letters. To check if two names match, you also make every letter small and then see if they are exactly the same.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists ten sample nicknames and the output used for comparison. Foo and foo both become foo, and Foo Bar becomes foo bar. Richard Ⅳ becomes richard iv, because lowercasing gives the small roman numeral (U+2173) and NFKC turns it into the letters i and v.

The Greek letters show the edge cases. Capital sigma (U+03A3) and small sigma (U+03C3) match after lowercasing, but final sigma (U+03C2) is not changed by toLowerCase(), so it matches neither of them. The symbol ∞ (U+221E) is allowed by the FreeformClass and may be used in nicknames.

One example shows non-idempotence. GREEK UPSILON WITH DIARESIS AND HOOK SYMBOL (U+03D4) is unchanged by lowercasing, but NFKC turns it into a capital letter (U+03AB). A second pass lowercases that to U+03CB.
sections.eli5: Big and small versions of a letter count as the same, so Foo and foo match. But a few special letters, like the Greek ending sigma, have their own look and do not match.

sections.title: Application Protocols and the PRECIS Registry
sections.content:
The RFC defines only the string-handling rules. Each application protocol, such as MSRP, XCON or XMPP, must say where nicknames appear, who enforces the rules and when. It may add its own rules, such as minimum or maximum length, extra code point restrictions, safeguards for look-alike characters, reserved nicknames or handling of duplicates. Enforcing entities are encouraged to be liberal: map characters where possible and accept the result, and reject only when mapping is not possible, for example because a character is disallowed.

IANA added a Nickname entry to the PRECIS Profiles registry. Its base class is FreeformClass, it has no width mapping or directionality rule, and its enforcement is left to applications.
sections.eli5: This rulebook only says how to tidy names. Each app decides where names go and whether to add its own rules, like a maximum length.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A nickname is a personally memorable handle for something with a more stable identity, such as a URI or a file path. Authentication and authorization decisions MUST be made on the basis of that identity, not the nickname.

The security considerations in RFC 8264 apply to the FreeformClass, and those in Unicode Technical Standard #39 apply to the use of Unicode code points. The mapping rules reduce the chance of confusion about nicknames, but the RFC does not give detailed advice on visually similar characters (confusables).
sections.eli5: A nickname is only a label. Never decide who gets into the clubhouse by the name on the label; check who the person really is.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7700
sections.content: This RFC replaces RFC 7700. It addresses an erratum by removing the directionality rule from the enforcement and comparison sections. It also replaces the Unicode toCaseFold() operation with toLowerCase(), following working group discussion and updates to RFC 8264. Other changes are editorial clarifications and updated references.
sections.eli5: This is a new edition of the rulebook. It drops one rule that was not needed and swaps how letters are made small.

viz.caption: THE FIVE RULES OF THE NICKNAME PROFILE

items.title: Additional mapping
items.text: Non-ASCII spaces to SPACE, trim ends, collapse runs.

items.title: Case mapping
items.text: Unicode toLowerCase(), used only for comparison.
